question: Why does a moving clock tick slowly?

research.claim: A clock that moves relative to an observer is measured by that observer to tick more slowly than identical clocks at rest, by the factor 1/γ = √(1 − v²/c²). A light clock shows why: its light keeps the one speed c that every observer measures, but seen from the observer it must travel a longer, slanted path between the moving mirrors, so each tick takes longer.
research.explanation: A light clock is two parallel mirrors a distance L apart with a flash of light bouncing between them; each crossing is one tick, taking L/c for a clock at rest. Put the clock on a rocket moving sideways at speed v. Seen from Earth, the mirrors move during each crossing, so the light must travel a slanted path to hit them. In time Δt′ it covers c Δt′ along the slant while the mirrors move v Δt′ sideways, so (c Δt′)² = L² + (v Δt′)², which gives Δt′ = (L/c)/√(1 − v²/c²) = γ L/c. The light's speed cannot change, since light has the same speed for every observer (the result of the Michelson–Morley experiment of 1887 and many later tests), so the longer path takes longer and the moving clock ticks slower as measured from Earth. Every kind of clock on the rocket, atomic, mechanical or biological, must slow by the same factor, or the crew could tell from their own clocks that they were moving, which the principle of relativity forbids. On board, the crew see their own clock tick normally, and they find Earth's clocks to be the slow ones: the effect is reciprocal while both coast. At 60% of light speed γ = 1.25, so the rocket clock ticks 8 times for every 10 on Earth; at 90%, γ ≈ 2.29, so it ticks fewer than half as often. At speeds far below light’s, γ is extremely close to 1, but precise clocks still show the effect: GPS satellite clocks, moving at about 4 km/s, run slow by about 7.2 microseconds a day from their speed alone. Near light speed the effect is large: muons at 98% of light speed live about five times longer than at rest.
assumptions: Special relativity: flat spacetime, no gravity (GPS clocks also have a larger, opposite gravitational effect, which is a separate idea).
Both clocks move at constant velocity; no acceleration or turnaround is treated (that is the twin paradox, another guide).
An ideal light clock whose light crosses at right angles to the motion in its own rest frame.
Light has the same speed for every inertial observer.
The tick counts compare the two clocks in the frame named on the stage: Earth’s, or the rocket’s in chapter 4.
The mirrors’ separation, at right angles to the motion, is the same for both observers, so the same L appears in both frames.
research.prediction: With γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²): at v = 0.6c, γ = 1.25 and the rocket clock ticks 8 times for every 10 Earth ticks (20% slower); at v = 0.9c, γ ≈ 2.294 and it ticks about 4.4 times for every 10 (about 56% slower); at v = 0 the clocks agree. At GPS orbital speed (v ≈ 3.87 km/s), v²/2c² ≈ 8.3 × 10⁻¹¹, a loss of about 7.2 μs per day from speed alone (gravity adds about +45.8 μs per day, for a net gain of about 38.6 μs per day). A muon at 98% of light speed (γ ≈ 5) lives about five times its 2.2 μs rest lifetime.
research.falsifier: Fast unstable particles (cosmic-ray muons, muons in storage rings) living no longer than slow ones; atomic clocks flown around the world showing no motion-dependent difference from clocks on the ground; or satellite navigation staying accurate without the speed part of its clock correction (about 7 μs a day).
limitations: Special relativity only: gravitational time dilation, which dominates GPS's net clock correction, is not shown.
Constant speeds only; what happens when a clock turns around and returns (the twin paradox) is not covered.
Chapter 4 draws the rocket’s view; the other chapters and the controls show the clocks as measured from Earth.
misconceptions: The moving clock is broken, or its mechanism is disturbed by the motion. (No: it ticks normally for anyone moving with it.)
It is just an illusion caused by light taking time to reach you. (No: the slowing is what synchronized clocks measure after allowing for travel time; fast muons really do last longer.)
The crew feel time dragging. (No: everything on board slows together, so they notice nothing.)
Only light clocks slow down. (No: every kind of clock, including the crew's bodies, slows by the same factor.)
If Earth sees the rocket clock slow, the crew must see Earth's clock fast. (No: while both coast, each finds the other's clock slow.)

questions.q: Why does the rocket clock tick slower when seen from Earth?
questions.a: Its light must travel a longer, slanted path to hit the moving mirrors, and its light keeps the same speed, so each tick takes longer.

questions.q: Do the crew feel time passing slowly?
questions.a: No. Seen from Earth, every clock on board, including their bodies, slows the same way, so to the crew their own clock looks normal.

questions.q: What happens when the rocket stops?
questions.a: Its light goes straight up and down again and it ticks at Earth’s rate, but it stays behind by the ticks it missed.

questions.q: Is the slowing just an illusion caused by light delay?
questions.a: No. It is what clocks measure: muons at 98% of light speed live about five times longer, and GPS satellite clocks lose about 7 millionths of a second a day from their speed.

questions.q: Why don't we notice it in everyday life?
questions.a: At everyday speeds the slant is tiny, so the slowing is far too small to notice, though precise clocks can measure it.

sources.title: Time dilation (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: A clock moving relative to an observer is measured to tick more slowly; the light-clock derivation (the moving clock's light travels the longer path D > L, so its ticks are longer); the effect is reciprocal; it applies to every kind of clock; a cosmic-ray muon at 98% of light speed lives about five times longer, in agreement with observations; satellite navigation must account for it.

sources.title: Error analysis for the Global Positioning System (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Clocks at GPS orbital speed (about 4 km/s) tick slower by about v²/2c² ≈ 10⁻¹⁰, an error of about −7.2 μs per day; gravity makes them faster by about +45.8 μs per day; combined, they gain about 38.6 μs per day.

sources.title: Muon (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: The muon's mean lifetime is 2.2 μs; the Rossi–Hall experiment (1941) used muons to observe the time dilation predicted by special relativity for the first time.

sources.title: Hafele–Keating experiment (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Atomic clocks flown around the world on airliners disagreed with clocks on the ground when reunited, consistent with the predictions of special and general relativity.

sources.title: Michelson–Morley experiment (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: The 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment found no difference in light’s speed along and across Earth’s motion; repeated with rising precision, it is one of the fundamental tests of special relativity, with the Kennedy–Thorndike and Ives–Stilwell experiments.

sources.title: What is the experimental basis of Special Relativity? (T. Roberts and S. Schleif, Usenet Physics FAQ)
sources.supports: Lists the tests of light’s constant speed since Michelson–Morley (1887), Kennedy–Thorndike and moving-source experiments, and the tests of time dilation (Ives and Stilwell, particle lifetimes, Doppler-shift measurements) and of the twin paradox (Hafele and Keating, Bailey et al.).

scene.title: Why does a moving clock tick slowly?
scene.subtitle: Build a clock from light bouncing between two mirrors, then put it on a fast rocket. Seen from Earth, the clock’s light takes a longer, slanted path at the same speed, so it ticks slower.
scene.why: Moving clocks really do tick slowly, and GPS satellites are built to allow for it. The reason is that light has one speed for everyone, as experiments since 1887 have shown.
scene.opening: Can a perfectly good clock run slow just because it is moving?

beats.title: A clock made of light
beats.body: Imagine a clock made of light: a flash bouncing between two mirrors. Each trip from one mirror to the other is one tick. At rest, two of these clocks tick in step.

beats.title: Put one on a rocket
beats.body: Now put one clock on a rocket going 60% of light speed. Seen from Earth, the rocket’s mirrors keep moving sideways. So the light must slant to hit them, taking a longer zigzag path.

beats.title: Light keeps one speed
beats.body: Light keeps the same speed for everyone, even on a moving rocket. So each trip along the longer path takes more time. The rocket clock ticks 8 times for every 10 on Earth.

beats.title: Seen from the rocket
beats.body: Seen from the rocket, its own clock ticks normally. Earth’s clock flies past, so its light slants. To the crew, Earth’s clock is the slow one.

beats.title: Near light speed
beats.body: The faster the rocket, the longer the slanted path. At 90% of light speed, the rocket clock slows by more than half. At GPS satellite speeds, clocks lose 7 millionths of a second a day.

scene.takeaway: A moving clock’s light must take a longer, slanted path, and light has one speed for everyone, so each tick takes longer. Every kind of clock slows the same way.

questions.q: What happens when the rocket stops?

questions.q: Is the slowing just an illusion caused by light delay?
questions.a: No. It is what clocks measure: muons at 98% of light speed live about five times longer, and GPS satellite clocks lose about 7 millionths of a second a day from their speed.

questions.q: Why don't we notice it in everyday life?

physics_review.summary: The guide, research record and engine agree with each other and with special relativity: the light paths, the tick ratios (8 per 10 at 60% of light speed; 4.4 per 10 and 56% slower at 90%), the rocket's view in chapter 4, the GPS figures (v²/2c² ≈ 8.3 × 10⁻¹¹ at 3.87 km/s, about −7.2 μs a day from speed, +45.8 μs from gravity, +38.6 μs net) and the muon figures (γ ≈ 5, 2.2 μs) all check out against the code, the frames and the saved sources. The hold at the stage edge freezes both clocks at the same Earth time, so the ratio stays exact.
changes: Round 1 caught 'the steeper the slant' (backwards) and a takeaway that gave the wrong cause for the longer path; both were fixed.
Round 2 caught research lines that still described the old picture; they were updated.

visual_review.summary: Every frame matches its subtitle. Chapter 4 is drawn from the rocket's view (the rocket's clock still, Earth's clock flying past with slanted light, 'Earth clock ticks slower by 20%'); counters sit clear of mirrors and light on desktop and on 320 to 430 px phones; the 90% picture holds on its full path through the last sentence and after playback; the ratio pill arrives with the sentence that states it; and the end card reads as plain text.
changes: Round 1 and round 2 failures (a chapter showing the opposite of its subtitles; counters on the light on phones; a restart mid-sentence) were fixed.
Round 3 caught an end card that printed code; it was fixed, a render check now guards it, and the reviewer confirmed the fix.

learner_review.summary: The idea: a clock moving past you ticks slower because, seen from where you stand, its light has to zigzag along a longer, slanted path at light's one fixed speed; it matters because the slowing is real for every kind of clock, and GPS satellites are built to allow for it. A first-time reader can fully explain why the rocket clock is slow, and nearly every line reads like spoken English and matches its picture.
changes: Small copy edits: 'At rest, two of these clocks tick in step.', 'Seen from Earth, the rocket’s mirrors keep moving sideways.', 'Earth’s clock flies past, so its light slants.', a GPS line that breaks at its comma.

blind_review.summary: From the pictures alone: two identical light clocks keep the same time when both stand still; seen from Earth, the moving rocket's light travels a longer slanted path between its mirrors, so its clock ticks less often (8 to Earth's 10); seen from the rocket, it is Earth's clock that slants and runs slow by the same amount; and at a higher speed the path slants more and the slowdown grows (4.4 to 10).
changes: Round 1 caught numbers that disagreed in the last chapter; the pill now shows one decimal and the counters are left out while the speed changes.
